content: 1. Are the key factors of vulnerability being addressed in the provision of services? This includes considerations of gender, human rights, and equity. 2. Are the products and services being produced in sufficient quantities? For example: The number of health facilities providing safe male circumcision services. The number of facilities offering all components of the minimum package of care for male circumcision services. 3. Is there sufficient uptake of male circumcision services by the intended populations? This can be measured by the proportion of males circumcised within the target population. 4. What types of human resources for health (HRH) are necessary for effective and efficient HIV/AIDS services? This includes physicians, nurses, midwives, lab technicians, community health workers (CHWs), etc. 5. Are there policies, strategies, and plans in place for skill mix (e.g., task shifting and task sharing)? Has the implementation of these policies and strategies been carried out effectively? 6. Have training and supervision of health workers been conducted to ensure access to HIV-related services? This includes: Incentives and compensation benefit packages. Obligations and regulations for health workers. 7. Is there an appropriate indicator package in place? Are the indicators consistent with the priorities of the strategic and operational plans? Are timely and appropriate training programs on HIV information being conducted? 8. Are there adequately available tools and equipment for managing HIV strategic information? Is there regular supportive supervision on monitoring and evaluation (M&E)? Is there capacity in core health information sciences (e.g., epidemiology, demography, statistics, information, and ICT)? 9. Is evidence being used to inform policies, strategies, and plans for the national HIV/AIDS program? Is data being utilized to estimate the effectiveness and impacts of the national HIV/AIDS program? 10. Are the national antiretroviral therapy (ART) guidelines aligned with the WHO’s latest progress and guidance on HIV treatment? This includes: The use of Fixed Dose Combination (FDC) drugs. The phase-out of d4T. CD4 count thresholds (e.g., <500). 11. Are cheaper antiretroviral drugs (ARVs) registered to enable procurement? If not, are there waiver clauses or an exceptionally accelerated registration process in place? 12. Is there a regulatory framework for commodity selection criteria? For example: The presence of a logistics task force responsible for inventory stock data analysis, procurement, and funding for procurement and supply management (PSM). The type of ARV toxicity reporting system (e.g., targeted spontaneous reporting, pregnancy registries, cohort event monitoring). The presence of a link between toxicity reporting systems and national guidelines committees for ART and PMTCT/eMTCT. 13. How do financial inputs relate to the results achieved by the program? Are cost-effectiveness analyses being conducted? 14. How is HIV contributing to health challenges in the country? This includes examining the roles of the public sector, private sector, non-governmental organizations, academia, and development partners. 15. Is there regular monitoring and supervision of the program? Are there links between the health strategy and the HIV strategy? Is the HIV Strategic Plan jointly assessed? Are there regular operational and implementation plans? 16. Are community organizations being supported to deliver and use quality services? This includes: M&E staff in community organizations. Exchange visits and peer-to-peer learning and support on community M&E. National plans, strategies, and policies relevant to communities. Community-level M&E and operational plans, including reporting systems. Regular supervision, mentoring, and feedback to community actors and stakeholders. 17. Are leadership, governance, and management structures in place to optimize HIV prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care outcomes? This includes: Male and female condom programming. Medical male circumcision. Services for key populations. Prevention among sero-discordant couples. Prevention of sexual transmission of HIV.
